1317.title: The Falcon Folds Its Wings
1317.hook: deep sleep leaves nothing to tell at breakfast; Yajnavalkya describes it anyway, with a falcon, and finds the self under every role
1317.carry: atman rests beneath every role you play
1317.tomorrow: Indra called deep sleep nothing. was he right?
1317.howItsDone: Vedanta teachers study deep, dreamless sleep, sushupti, beside waking and dreaming, and read Yajnavalkya's falcon as a picture of the self at rest.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-SEVENTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the dreamer: the self is its own light, making chariots and rivers where there are none.
screen: `SELF-LIT.`

segments.voice: Deep sleep is the one part of the night with nothing to report. No dream to tell over breakfast. Just a gap, and then the alarm. A gap seems an odd thing to teach. The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad tries anyway. Yajnavalkya, still talking with King Janaka, has walked through waking and through dreams. Now he goes one step further down, and to describe it, he reaches for a bird. Today, the sleep with no dreams in it.
screen: `NOTHING TO REPORT.` → `A GAP, THEN THE ALARM.` → `ONE STEP FURTHER DOWN.`

segments.voice: Here's the bird, paraphrased. A falcon, or an eagle, has been flying in the open sky. It's tired, so it folds its wings and drops to its nest. In the same way, a person hurries toward that state where, asleep, he wants nothing at all and sees no dream. Then Yajnavalkya says something stranger. There, a father is not a father, a mother is not a mother. The worlds are not worlds, the gods not gods, the Vedas not Vedas. A thief is not a thief. He is untouched by good and untouched by evil, the text says, for he has crossed over all the sorrows of the heart. Three things. First, the folded wings. The falcon isn't defeated. It flew all day; folding the wings is just the other half of flying. Second, the roles. Every name a person carries by day, parent, worker, friend, even the one with a past, is set down in deep sleep. Not erased. Set down. And here is the teaching, named plainly: the self, atman, is not any of those roles. It carries them by day, and it's what remains when they're put down. Third, the sorrows of the heart. The text doesn't say grief is cured, only that, in that state, the sleeper has crossed over it. And for honesty: Yajnavalkya isn't saying the goal of life is to sleep well. Deep sleep, for him, is a clue, a nightly taste of the self without wanting. The Mandukya Upanishad lines up waking, dreaming and deep sleep, and points past all of them.
screen: `THE FALCON FOLDS ITS WINGS` · `A FATHER IS NOT A FATHER` · `ATMAN: NOT ANY ROLE` · `A CLUE, NOT THE GOAL`

segments.voice: Name, silently, one role you carried today, parent, worker, friend, student, the one who has to answer, and with the next breath out set it down beside you, not thrown away, just put down. Then the next, and when there are no more names, rest in whatever is left. If you pray, rest in prayer there.
Sleep. In deep sleep, the Brihadaranyaka says, a person wants nothing, sees no dream, and has crossed the sorrows of the heart, like a falcon folding its wings. Today's word.

1318.title: Indra Asks About Deep Sleep
1318.hook: Indra studies the self for a hundred and one years and nearly quits over deep sleep; the morning's 'I slept well' says someone was there
1318.carry: the self is the witness, even in deep sleep
1318.tomorrow: Kumbhakarna woke and told the king the truth. then what?
1318.howItsDone: Vedanta teachers read Indra's long stay with Prajapati as a lesson in how to look for the self, and point to deep sleep and the morning's 'I slept well' to teach atman as the witness, sakshi; students of the Yoga Sutras learn sleep as one of the five vrittis.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-EIGHTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the falcon folded its wings: atman rests beneath every role you play, every daytime name set down.
screen: `THE FALCON FOLDS ITS WINGS.`

segments.voice: Indra, king of the gods, wants to know the self. In the Chandogya Upanishad he goes to Prajapati, the creator, and lives with him as a student for thirty-two years. He's taught, he leaves, he doubts, he comes back. It happens again. The third time, Prajapati points him to deep, dreamless sleep. And Indra, halfway home, stops on the road. Paraphrased: in that state a person doesn't even know, 'this is me.' It's as if he's gone to nothing. I see no good in this. Today, the king of the gods against the gap in the night.
screen: `THE KING OF THE GODS, A STUDENT.` → `THIRTY-TWO YEARS, THEN AGAIN.` → `I SEE NO GOOD IN THIS.`

segments.voice: Prajapati doesn't scold him. He says: stay five more years. Indra's whole stay comes to a hundred and one years, the text says, for one teaching. And the teaching, paraphrased: this body is mortal, held by death, but it's the dwelling of a self that is deathless and without a body. Another school asks the same question. Patanjali's Yoga Sutras count sleep among the mind's five movements: a turning that rests on absence. And the commentary credited to Vyasa notices the morning. On waking, a person says, I slept well, my mind is clear. Or, I slept badly, my mind is dull. You can't remember what never happened to you, so something was there. Here is the teaching, named plainly. Vedanta teachers call it the witness, sakshi: the self, atman, that sees waking, sees dreams, and is present even when there is nothing to see. Many teachers read the morning's 'I slept well' as the witness's fingerprint. You can't look at it, which is exactly why Indra kept missing it: it's the one doing the looking. That's why, in this teaching, you aren't your moods or your nights. Light and heavy, clear and dull, they come and go, and the witness sees them all. And as with every day in this lens: the texts describe the mind; they don't diagnose sleep. Heavy nights and dull mornings for a long stretch are a conversation for a doctor.
screen: `A HUNDRED AND ONE YEARS FOR ONE TEACHING` · `I SLEPT WELL: SOMEONE WAS THERE` · `SAKSHI: THE WITNESS` · `YOU AREN'T YOUR MOODS OR NIGHTS`

segments.voice: Go back to last night's sleep, not the hours but the quality, light or heavy, clear or tangled, and find one honest word for it. Then notice: something just remembered a night you were supposedly absent for. Rest a few breaths as the one who notices, not as the night. If you pray, give thanks for whatever rest there was.
Sleep. For Indra, a gap that looked like nothing; in the Yoga Sutras, a turning of the mind remembered in the morning; for Vedanta, a night the witness sees. Today's word.

1319.title: Kumbhakarna Tells the Truth
1319.hook: drums, conches and elephants wake a giant; he tells his brother the king the truth, and then has to choose
1319.carry: dharma is knowing the right, then choosing it
1319.tomorrow: why does a temple sing God awake each morning?
1319.howItsDone: Kumbhakarna and Vibhishana are retold in Ramayana tellings and Ramlila performances, and on Dussehra many towns in North India burn effigies of Ravana, Kumbhakarna and Meghanada.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-NINETEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Indra's lesson: the self is the witness, even in deep sleep, or the morning couldn't say I slept well.
screen: `SAKSHI: THE WITNESS.`

segments.voice: Drums are pounding. Conches are blowing. People are shouting into a giant's ears, and elephants are being led over his sleeping body. Next to him, food is heaped up for the moment his eyes open. It's Lanka, in Valmiki's Ramayana, and the city is under siege. Ravana needs his brother Kumbhakarna, and Kumbhakarna is asleep. Getting him up takes a crowd. Today, what a giant says when he finally wakes, and what he does next.
screen: `DRUMS, CONCHES, ELEPHANTS.` → `A CITY UNDER SIEGE.` → `THE GIANT IS ASLEEP.`

segments.voice: We met Kumbhakarna's sleep earlier this week: the boon that went wrong, tamas, the pull to stay under. Today is about him awake. He eats, he's brought to his brother, and Ravana tells him everything: the taking of Sita, the army at the walls. And the sleepy giant tells the king the truth to his face. Paraphrased: you did this without listening to counsel; you did first what should have come after. He isn't the first to say it. Their younger brother Vibhishana had already told Ravana: give Sita back. Ravana insulted him, and Vibhishana left and crossed over to Rama. So the Ramayana sets three brothers side by side. Ravana knows, and won't listen. Vibhishana knows, and acts, and it costs him his home. Kumbhakarna knows, says it plainly, and then goes out to fight for his brother anyway, and falls to Rama. Here is the teaching, named plainly: dharma, what's right, isn't only something you know. It's something you choose. Kumbhakarna's honesty is real, and many retellings honor his loyalty. But the tradition still remembers which side he chose. On Dussehra, in many towns in North India, Ravana's giant effigy burns, and beside it, Kumbhakarna's and Meghanada's. And Vibhishana, the one who walked out, is the one Rama makes king of Lanka. The today step is hard and familiar: knowing someone you love is wrong, and standing with them anyway. The Ramayana doesn't say love your family less. It says loyalty doesn't make the wrong thing right. And one careful note: tiredness that won't lift is a matter for a doctor, never a mark of bad character.
screen: `YOU ACTED WITHOUT COUNSEL` · `THREE BROTHERS, ONE CHOICE` · `DHARMA: KNOWN, THEN CHOSEN` · `LOYALTY DOESN'T MAKE WRONG RIGHT`

segments.voice: Let one place come to mind where you know what's right and haven't chosen it yet, maybe with someone you love. Let it sit in front of you while you breathe, without scolding yourself. Then find the smallest step that would choose it, one sentence or one look, and hold it lightly. If you pray, say Rama's name softly, Shri Ram, and ask for Vibhishana's courage; if you don't, just hold the step.
Sleep. Kumbhakarna's long sleep, and his waking: the truth told plainly, and the choice he made after. Today's word.

1320.title: Rama, the Dawn Is Breaking
1320.hook: a sage wakes two sleeping princes by a river, and his words become a temple's dawn song for the Lord
1320.carry: hindu worship cares for god, dawn to night
1320.tomorrow: what happened the day the wind stopped blowing?
1320.howItsDone: The Venkatesa Suprabhatam is sung at dawn at the Tirumala temple and played in homes in the morning, and some temples close the day with a rite that lays the deity to rest.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-TWENTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kumbhakarna woke and told the king the truth: dharma is knowing the right, then choosing it.
screen: `KNOWN, THEN CHOSEN.`

segments.voice: Before sunrise, by a river, two young princes are asleep on the ground. The sage leading them, Vishvamitra, leans over and speaks. Paraphrased: Rama, fortunate son of Kausalya, the eastern dawn is breaking. Rise, tiger among men; the day's rites are waiting. It's a small moment early in Valmiki's Ramayana, a teacher waking his students. But those words didn't stay by the river. They became the opening of a hymn sung before dawn to wake the deity. Today, the last of the sleep days: the temple's night and morning.
screen: `TWO PRINCES ASLEEP BY A RIVER.` → `RAMA, THE DAWN IS BREAKING.` → `A HYMN TO WAKE GOD.`

segments.voice: The hymn is the Venkatesa Suprabhatam, sung at dawn at the Venkateswara temple at Tirumala. Suprabhatam means a good dawn. It opens with Vishvamitra's verse, then turns to the Lord of the hill and asks him, verse after verse, to wake. At the other end of the day, some temples have a bedtime rite. The deity is laid to rest, the lamps are lowered, a last song is sung, and the doors are shut until morning. Here is the teaching, named plainly. In Hindu worship the deity in the temple is treated as truly present, so the whole day is seva, loving service: woken, bathed, offered food, and laid to rest. Tradition speaks of these rites as care, not as a claim that God gets tired: the way a beloved member of the household is served. Two more things to see. The waking is spoken. Vishvamitra doesn't shake the princes. He tells them the dawn is here and the day has work in it. And the two ends of the day frame everything between. Look back over the sleep days. Kumbhakarna slept his strength away, and the Gita asked for measure. Uddalaka's bird settled at its tether. Yajnavalkya's dreamer was self-lit; his falcon folded its wings, and every daytime name was set down. Indra nearly quit over deep sleep, and found the witness. Kumbhakarna woke and knew the right. And here, the night and the dawn held as worship. Tomorrow, the breath, and the day the wind god stood still.

1321.title: The Day the Wind Stopped
1321.hook: baby Hanuman leaps for the sun, Indra strikes him down, and the wind god stops: every creature chokes
1321.carry: pranayama tends breath as a sacred gift
1321.tomorrow: speech, mind or breath: who really holds the body up?
1321.howItsDone: Hanuman's leap at the sun is told to Hindu children in Ramayana retellings, and some yoga teachers who follow Patanjali have students watch the breath before regulating it, adapting or skipping breath-holding for students with health conditions.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-TWENTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Last week closed on Hindu worship caring for God, dawn to night: a temple's bedtime and its dawn song, and Rama woken with words.
screen: `RAMA, THE DAWN IS BREAKING.`

segments.voice: A baby wakes up hungry. Above him, the rising sun glows red, and he thinks it's a fruit. So he jumps for it. This is Hanuman, son of Vayu, the wind, and in the Ramayana's telling he leaps right up into the sky. Indra, king of the gods, alarmed, strikes him with his thunderbolt, and the child falls onto a mountain, his jaw broken. Then his father does something terrible and quiet. Vayu stops. Today, the day the wind stopped blowing, and what it teaches about breath.
screen: `A BABY JUMPS FOR THE SUN.` → `THE THUNDERBOLT.` → `THE WIND STOPS.`

segments.voice: Vayu, grieving, takes his son into a cave and holds still. And because the wind is also the breath in every body, everything chokes. Creatures can't breathe, the text says; their bodies go stiff like wood; the gods themselves are in distress. They run to Brahma, the creator, who comes to the cave and revives the child, and the wind moves again. Then the gods, one by one, give Hanuman boons, and the Ramayana ties his name to that broken jaw, hanu. Here is the teaching, named plainly. In Hindu thought, breath isn't just air. Vayu is a god, and prana, breath, is life itself, given to every body. That's why yoga treats breath with care. Patanjali's Yoga Sutras make breath practice, pranayama, one of yoga's eight limbs, and describe it simply: the breath out, the breath in and the pause, watched by place, by time and by number, becomes long and fine. That's a description, not a promise. It doesn't say a pattern heals illness, and it gives no count of seconds. So this week, every claim about breath gets one of three labels: the text says, tradition says, or a doctor decides. One plain safety line, because breath work isn't neutral. Anyone with a heart or lung condition, anyone pregnant, anyone who gets dizzy or anxious with breath exercises keeps to easy natural breathing and asks a doctor before any holding of the breath. Today's practice holds nothing. It only watches, the way you'd look after a gift.
screen: `THE WIND STOPS; EVERYTHING CHOKES` · `VAYU: BREATH AS A GOD` · `PRANAYAMA: ONE OF EIGHT LIMBS` · `TEXT, TRADITION, OR A DOCTOR`

segments.voice: Let the breath do whatever it's doing, and watch it by place, where it's felt most, then by time, whether the in-breath runs longer than the out-breath, then by number, counting a few breaths from one to five, without changing anything. If it grows longer and finer on its own, notice that; if it doesn't, that's an honest result too. If you pray, let each out-breath be a small thanks to the One who gives it.
The breath again. When Vayu stood still, every creature choked; in the Yoga Sutras, breath watched by place, time and number becomes long and fine. Today's word.
screen: `THE BREATH AGAIN — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: pranayama tends breath as a sacred gift. The text says, tradition says, a doctor decides. That's today, done.

1322.title: The Senses Quarrel With Breath
1322.hook: the senses quarrel over who holds the body up, and breath settles it by getting up to leave
1322.carry: prana holds the body; the senses follow
1322.tomorrow: where does breath come from? a student asks too much.
1322.howItsDone: Hindu teachers read the Prashna Upanishad's quarrel of the senses as a teaching about what keeps a being alive, and some Hindus sit with the breath as a daily practice of attention.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-TWENTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the wind stopped and every creature choked: pranayama tends breath as a sacred gift.
screen: `THE WIND STOPS.`

segments.voice: An argument breaks out inside a body. Speech says it holds the body up. So does the mind. So do the eye and the ear. Each one is sure it's the pillar. Then breath, the quiet one, says nothing much. It just starts to leave. And the moment it lifts, every other power is dragged up with it, whether it likes it or not. This story sits in the second question of the Prashna Upanishad, a text built as six students asking a teacher six questions. Today: what it means by breath, and one popular claim, checked against the page.
screen: `AN ARGUMENT INSIDE A BODY.` → `BREATH STARTS TO LEAVE.` → `ONE CLAIM, CHECKED AGAINST THE PAGE.`

segments.voice: Here's the scene, in paraphrase. A student asks the teacher Pippalada which powers hold a being together, and which of them is greatest. The teacher tells the quarrel. The elements and the senses each claim the body. Breath warns them not to be fooled: it alone, dividing itself, keeps the body standing. They don't believe it. So breath rises to go, and they all rise with it. It settles, and they all settle, like bees following their king bee out of the hive and back again. Then the senses sing to breath, and the hymn makes it very large. Breath burns as fire, shines as the sun, falls as rain. Breath is in everything. Now the claim. You'll hear in wellness writing that prana is basically oxygen, or that it's a hidden energy a machine can read. The first is too small: the Prashna's breath is fire and rain and the life of creatures, not one gas in the lungs. The second is a different kind of claim altogether. The Upanishad never offers prana as something to measure. It offers a way of seeing a living thing as held together by something it doesn't control. Here is the teaching, named plainly: prana is life itself, the power that holds a being together, and every sense, even the mind, follows where it goes. It's a teaching about life, not a reading on a dial. What a person can actually watch is the breath itself, going out and coming back. The Prashna asks for nothing more.
screen: `THE SENSES EACH CLAIM THE BODY` · `BEES FOLLOWING THEIR KING BEE` · `BREATH AS FIRE, SUN AND RAIN` · `A TEACHING, NOT A READING ON A DIAL`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath rise and settle without steering it. As it rises, notice what rises with it, the chest, the shoulders, maybe a thought; as it settles, let speech go quiet and the eyes rest, the swarm following its king bee. If you pray, you can offer one breath back with thanks.
The breath again. In the Prashna, breath gets up to leave and every other power rises with it, like bees with their king. Today's word.

1323.title: Kausalya Asks Too Much
1323.hook: a student asks one question too many about breath, and the teacher answers anyway, with a king and his officers
1323.carry: breath is the self's shadow, not the self
1323.tomorrow: patanjali's word for good breath isn't 'deep'. what is it?
1323.howItsDone: Teachers of yoga and Ayurveda use the names prana, apana, samana, vyana and udana for movements of breath in the body, often as a way of paying attention rather than as anatomy, and some Hindu families offer the first grains of a meal to the five breaths.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-TWENTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, breath got up to leave and the senses rose with it like bees: prana holds the body; the senses follow.
screen: `THE BREATH AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Some questions go past the lesson plan. In the Prashna Upanishad, the third student asks one. His name is Kausalya, and he doesn't ask what breath is. He asks where it comes from, how it gets into the body, how it splits itself up, and how it leaves. The teacher's first reply, in paraphrase, is a raised eyebrow: you ask more than you should. Then he answers anyway, because the student is sincere. Today: the map he draws, and what that map is and isn't.
screen: `THE QUESTION PAST THE LESSON PLAN.` → `YOU ASK MORE THAN YOU SHOULD.` → `HE ANSWERS ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: Pippalada begins at the source. Breath, he says, is born from the self, the way a shadow falls from a person. It isn't the self; it's what the self casts. Breath works like a king who sends officers out to govern villages: you take this one, you take that one. One current, called apana, works low in the body, with elimination and birth. Breath proper, prana, lives in the eye and ear, the mouth and nose. Samana, in the middle, spreads what's eaten evenly, the way a fire is fed. Vyana moves through the body's channels. And udana rises, and at the end, the text says, carries a person on. Here is the teaching, named plainly: breath is not the self, atman. It's the self's shadow, and it serves like a king's officers. That's why some Hindu families, before eating, set aside a few grains and offer them to the five breaths by name, pranaya svaha, apanaya svaha, and the rest: the first of the meal goes to the officers. The Chandogya Upanishad describes that offering to the breaths. Now the claim. Online, the five winds are sometimes described as organs you could point to on a scan. The Prashna offers pictures, a king and a shadow, chosen to teach. Ayurveda's classical texts use the same names for movement in the body, read on this path as a way of noticing, never a diagnosis. And one more thing the text models: a hard question is welcome. The teacher grumbles, then gives his best answer.
screen: `BREATH FALLS FROM THE SELF LIKE A SHADOW` · `A KING SENDS OFFICERS TO THE VILLAGES` · `PRANAYA SVAHA: THE FIRST BITES` · `A MAP OF MOVEMENT, NOT A SCAN`

segments.voice: Let the breath come on its own and, for a few breaths, notice anything settling downward, the weight of the body on the seat; then the spreading, warmth or ease moving out from the middle; then the small lift at the top of each breath in. You're not finding organs, only noticing movement, the way the old map invites. If you pray, you can let one breath be a quiet thanks.
The breath again. In the Prashna, breath falls from the self like a shadow and sends out officers, like a king. Today's word.
screen: `THE BREATH AGAIN — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: breath is the self's shadow, not the self. And questions past the lesson plan are welcome here. Back tomorrow, same hill.
